I ran out of searches before reaching bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org notes, the Catholic or Orthodox sites, or any pages from a specific denomination. The verse-by-verse notes below come mostly from older commentaries on Bible Hub and StudyLight, plus Enduring Word. The Enduring Word and Precept Austin pages were cut off before verse 37, so coverage of vv. 31–39 and vv. 53–59 is thin.

## 1. Traditional reading, verse by verse

**vv. 31–37 (sores in the hair or beard, with two seven-day waits)**
- Kelly sums up this section: if the sore wasn't deep, the priest waited, then waited again. Only if it still hadn't spread or deepened could he pronounce the person clean. if not so deep, he must delay, when if it did not spread nor deepen, he must delay again, and then if all went on thus favourably, he might pronounce him clean. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/13-40.html)
- Guzik says the method leaned toward safety. Anyone who couldn't be pronounced clean with certainty was isolated until they could be. The methodology erred on the side of safety (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-13/)
- Lesson from the waiting periods (an old sermon): if God wanted no haste in judging visible sores, He wants even less haste in judging our neighbours' unseen hearts. God would have no haste, but a stay for seven days, and longer as occasion served, before any judgment should be given (https://biblehub.com/sermons/leviticus/13-45.htm)
- On the "yellow hair" in vv. 32 and 36, Whedon quotes Dr. Davidson, a doctor who examined lepers in Madagascar. He found that hair on the affected spot turns yellow and stunted, then falls out. The hairs upon the part become yellow and stunted, and, after a time, fall off (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/leviticus-13.html)

**vv. 38–39 (dull white spots)**
- Matthew Henry reads vv. 38–41 as safeguards: freckled skin or a bald head should not be mistaken for leprosy. In his words, Every deformity must not forthwith be made a ceremonial defilement. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/13-40.html)
- Bell's Commentary identifies vv. 38–39 as white blotches or "tetter," a harmless skin rash. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cbb/leviticus-13.html)

**vv. 40–41 (baldness)**
- Ellicott: leprosy makes hair fall out around the spot, but baldness alone is no sign of it. Because a bald head is a common place for a leprous spot to appear, any eruption there still had to be tested. baldness is in itself no sign of leprosy, whether at the back or front of the head (https://biblehub.com/leviticus/13-40.htm)
- Baldness was often seen as a disgrace or even a punishment from God (2 Kings 2:23). Even so, simply losing hair was not to be taken as a sign of leprosy. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/13-40.htm)
- Keil & Delitzsch, Cambridge Bible and Gill all say v. 40 means baldness at the back of the head and v. 41 baldness at the front. Keil adds that both kinds were naturally clean. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/13-40.htm)
- Guzik notes that through the centuries this verse has comforted men who lose their hair. He also quotes Peter-Contesse: Hebrew had a separate word for forehead baldness, linked to the idea of a "high" forehead. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-13/)
- A modern study note: verse 40 kept people from being needlessly quarantined, and it stopped superstition about hair loss. (https://biblehub.com/leviticus/13-40.htm)

**vv. 42–44 (a reddish-white sore on a bald head)**
- Whedon: a reddish-white sore alone was a sure token of the dreadful disease. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/leviticus-13.html)
- Constable: baldness didn't make a person unclean, but a serious skin disease on the head did. He suggests psoriasis may be meant. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/13-40.html)
- Gill cites the Mishnah (early Jewish law): the two signs on a bald head were raw flesh and spreading. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/leviticus-13.html)
- Spiritual reading in Matthew Henry's concise commentary: if the "leprosy of sin" reaches the head, meaning a corrupted judgment and wicked principles, few are cleansed from it. Soundness in the faith keeps leprosy from the head. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/13-40.htm)

**v. 45 (torn clothes, loose hair, covered lip, "Unclean!")**
- Keil & Delitzsch: lepers had to dress as mourners and cry "Unclean" so that everyone would avoid them for fear of being made unclean (Lam. 4:15). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/13-45.htm)
- The commentary on that page explains that a leper made a house unclean just by entering it, so he had to warn passers-by. Sometimes a herald walked ahead of him, and the old Aramaic paraphrase (Targum Jonathan) reads it that way. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/13-45.htm)
- Two readings of the covered lip. Jamieson-Fausset-Brown say it means either wearing a moustache or just keeping a hand over the lip. Clarke says the jaws were tied with linen, the way Jews bound up the dead. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/13-45.htm; https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/erv/leviticus/13-45.html)
- Poole: the cry did three things. It begged others for pity and prayer, confessed his condition, and warned people to keep away. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/13-45.htm)
- Matthew Henry: the leprosy was not itself a sin, but it was a sign of God's displeasure. The leper had to humble himself and accept it. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/13-45.html)
- Guzik: once leprosy was confirmed, the person lived in permanent mourning and permanent public disgrace. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-13/)
- A contrast: Leviticus 10:6 forbade priests to tear their clothes, so the leper's look showed how far apart holy and unclean were. The modern Bible Hub note links the cry to Isaiah 6:5 and to Christ's words, "I am willing; be cleansed." (https://biblehub.com/leviticus/13-45.htm)

**v. 46 (living alone outside the camp)**
- Peter-Contesse, quoted by Guzik: "alone" doesn't mean totally alone. People with the disease could live together, just away from everyone else (2 Kings 7:3–10). Guzik adds that by Jesus' time many Jews saw lepers as "the walking dead," punished by God. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-13/)
- Constable: the leper lived in an unclean area outside the camp, so he couldn't come near God, who lived in the tabernacle at the centre. He also compares this to Adam being driven out of Eden. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/13-46.html)
- Poole and Benson give three reasons for the rule: to humble the leper, to protect others from infection, and to show the danger of keeping company with notorious sinners. Matthew Henry says it typified the purity which ought to be in the gospel church. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/13-46.htm)
- Barnes: lepers probably still received sympathy and kindness, and they lived together (2 Kings 7:3; Luke 17:12). (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/13-46.htm)
- Modern study note: Christ "suffered outside the gate" (Heb. 13:12), taking the outsider's place. (https://biblehub.com/leviticus/13-46.htm)
- Old sermons use this verse for church discipline. Samuel Mather's outline simply labels it "Excommunication." (https://biblehub.com/sermons/leviticus/13-45.htm)

**vv. 47–49 (mildew in wool, linen or leather)**
- Matthew Henry admits this kind of "leprosy" in clothing is a thing which to us now is altogether unaccountable. (https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_013.cfm)
- Treasury of Scripture Knowledge records two views. Bishop Patrick saw it as a special punishment from God. Others think it had nothing to do with leprosy in people. (https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nlt/leviticus/13-47.html)
- Seiss thinks it was some problem in woven cloth that only looked like leprosy on the body. (https://biblehub.com/sermons/leviticus/13-47.htm)
- Gill: according to the Mishnah teachers, only wool and linen could be made unclean. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/13-47.html)

**vv. 50–52 (seven-day isolation; burning)**
- Here too, spreading is the deciding sign, as in a person. A leprous garment, like a leper, made anyone who touched it unclean. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/13-51.htm)
- Bell applies the burning in v. 52 to us: we too were headed for eternal fire, but Jesus rescued us. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cbb/leviticus-13.html)

**vv. 53–59 (washing, cutting out, burning)**
- Matthew Henry: a suspect garment was not burned straight away. Spiritually, sin brings a stain upon all he has and all that he does. (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/13-51.htm)
- Bridgeway summary: affected clothing had to be washed. If that didn't remove the problem, it had to be destroyed. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/13-45.html)
- Expositor's Bible looks ahead to the redeemed in white robes: No more leprosy then in person, house, or garment! (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/teb/leviticus-13.html)

## 2. Differences between Protestant traditions
I found none. Writers from very different backgrounds read these verses the same way, as a picture of sin. StudyLight labels them Gill (Baptist, Calvinist), Coffman (Restoration Movement, Arminian) and Constable (non-denominational, dispensational). (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/13-40.html)

The one real disagreement isn't between denominations. It's about why lepers and garments were excluded:
- **Not about contagion:** one commentary on v. 45 says the aim was to stop ceremonial uncleanness spreading, and to teach that unforgiven sin separates a person from God's people. (https://biblehub.com/leviticus/13-45.htm) Another note says the Jewish authorities did not treat leprosy as contagious. (https://biblehub.com/leviticus/13-47.htm) Whedon says many held it was handled on purely ceremonial grounds. (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/whe/leviticus-13.html)
- **About contagion:** Gill argued a leper's clothes really were infectious. (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/13-47.html) Guzik and Precept Austin treat the rules as real public health measures. (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_13_commentary)
